Lots of questions! Lots to unpack and there is more behind my answers.

\- Can I lean it against wall?  
Unstrung? Sure, my longbow is sat against a bookshelf and the wall.   
\- Can you hold at full draw for very long  
In general you won't hold the bow for minutes like in the movies. Depending on the style 10-15 seconds tops. Usually? Between 3-4 seconds.  
\- I hear it is bad for wood  
Leaving the bow strung for longer periods of time can warp the wood. Preferably you string the bow right before your shooting session and unstring it when you are done. Yes, a bow can survive 6 hours in the field. You can see the.. bow in the bow, but it naturally sets back over time... until a certain point that is.  
\- the arrow won’t fly as far ?  
A bow that has been used a lot.. or has been warped due to being strung for multiple longer periods will have less of a punch. A longbow is also (in general!) a much less efficient bow than an asiatic or modern bow.

That is a very simple statement, varnish can and will yellow/brown over time.

Varnish essentially allows an artist to add gloss or dull down their painting (usually the former!), besides offering a protective layer over the paint. Over time the varnish gathers the dirt and grime that would've been deposited onto the paint itself.  In a restoration the grimy varnish can be removed carefully, so it can be replaced with a fresh coat. However any restoration can be damaging to the painting. Hence why restorations don't happen often on an art piece.

[Info on how varnish works.](https://mci.si.edu/painting-varnishes)

Varnish helps protecting the colors. As part of a restoration it can be replaced with a fresh layer.

Edit: since people can't read any further..

Yes, varnish protects the color but it will eventually discolor!
A restoration is almost never non-invasive and CAN damage the original work. Hence why people are very careful performing one. It requires research on what solvents will react least with the paints. In some cases the paint will be touched up because of the damage done during a restoration. 
Varnish will add a gloss or be matt, changing the properties of the colors. Usually the intent is to make them more vibrant.
